reasons: No tests are visible in this file.
The migrations that must match these definitions are not in this file, so agreement cannot be checked here.
Several fields that should be fixed lists, such as company type and role, are stored as free text.

terms.meaning: A tool that describes database tables in code and runs queries against them.
A library that checks that data has the expected shape before the app uses it.
A lookup helper that makes searches on a column faster.
A column type that stores structured data inside the database as one block.
The column that uniquely identifies each row.
A numbered script that changes the real database so it matches these definitions.
Copied word for word from the original source.

used_by: database migrations (numbered, such as 0010, not in this file)

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports for table definitions
sections.what: Brings in the database tool, the column types, and the input checking tools used to define every table in the file.
sections.why: Likely reason: the file uses one library to define tables and another to build input checks.
sections.watch_out: Removing or renaming one of these imports breaks every table that uses it.

sections.name: projects (part 1)
sections.title: Main project table columns
sections.what: Defines the projects table, which holds one row per project. It stores name, description, budget, capacity, dates, status, lifecycle stage, maturity, parties, variances and a free-form attributes field.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the project facts the app shows together in one table so pages read a single row.
sections.watch_out: The older budget column is a float, while the planned and actual budget columns are exact numbers, and new code should use the exact ones.

sections.name: projects (part 2)
sections.title: Indexes that speed up project searches
sections.what: Creates lookup indexes on project status, lifecycle stage, maturity, country, industry, and key dates, so filters and sorts stay fast.
sections.why: Likely reason: the dashboard filters projects by these fields often.
sections.watch_out: Each index slows down inserts and updates, so adding many indexes can make large imports slower.

sections.name: evidenceQuotes
sections.title: Stored source quotes for projects
sections.what: Defines the table of verbatim source quotes, each linked to a project with its publisher, date, optional link, and the field it supports. It also records which rule found the quote and why a document is missing when there is none.
sections.why: The comments say these fields exist for traceability and for the verification rule.
sections.watch_out: Quotes link to a project by id only, with no foreign key, so a quote can point at a project that no longer exists.

sections.name: issues
sections.title: Stored problem notes for projects
sections.what: Defines the issues table. Each row names a project, its lifecycle stage, its impact, a description, and a list of evidence references.
sections.why: Likely reason: the app lists risks or problems per project from this table.
sections.watch_out: Evidence references are plain text ids with no link check, so they can point at quotes that do not exist.

sections.name: scorecardPillars
sections.title: Scorecard scores per project area
sections.what: Defines the table storing each scorecard area for a project, with its title, numeric score, trend, confidence, positives, negatives, evidence references, and matched SKU items.
sections.why: Likely reason: each project has several scored areas that appear together on its scorecard.
sections.watch_out: The SKU matches are loosely typed, so the database cannot catch a wrong shape there.

sections.name: maturityGates
sections.title: Stored status for each maturity gate
sections.what: Defines the table holding one row per project per gate, with status, score, rationale, verbatim evidence, source details, confidence, and a link to the evidence row. A unique rule allows only one row per project and gate.
sections.why: The comments say any status other than unknown must carry a verbatim quote, for traceability.
sections.watch_out: The rule that a non-unknown status needs a quote exists only as a comment, so the database does not enforce it.

sections.name: successStories
sections.title: Facts and takeaways per project
sections.what: Defines the table of facts and takeaways shown as a success story, holding one story per project.
sections.why: Likely reason: a project has a single story block on its page.
sections.watch_out: The project id is unique here, so saving a second story for the same project will fail.

sections.name: glossaryTerms
sections.title: Glossary entries with citations
sections.what: Defines the glossary table, with each term's definition, category, industry, and a list of citations holding titles, links, and excerpts. A term can appear only once per industry.
sections.why: Likely reason: each definition should point to a source, so the citations are stored with it.
sections.watch_out: Citations are stored as one block per term, so changing one citation means rewriting the whole list.

sections.name: milestones
sections.title: Project milestone dates
sections.what: Defines the table of key project milestones with planned and actual dates and a status.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the app compare planned and actual dates for each milestone.
sections.watch_out: Dates are stored as calendar dates, so a missing actual date stays empty rather than being estimated.

sections.name: projectUpdates
sections.title: Dated news about each project
sections.what: Defines the table of dated updates for a project, with headline, source, link, excerpt, and a locator that points at the spot in the source.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps a dated record of news so the app can show the latest events.
sections.watch_out: The publish time defaults to now when not given, which can make an older item look new.

sections.name: technologyDetails
sections.title: Reactor technical details per project
sections.what: Defines the table holding one technical summary per project: reactor type, thermal and electric capacity, fuel, design generation, and designer.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps technical facts apart from the main project table.
sections.watch_out: Capacity is stored as whole numbers, so fractional values may be rejected or rounded on save.

sections.name: skuMappings
sections.title: Links from projects to SKU categories
sections.what: Defines the table that links a project to a catalogue category, with a description and a whole-number alignment score.
sections.why: Likely reason: records how well each project matches a catalogue category.
sections.watch_out: The alignment score has no range check here, so an out-of-range score can be saved.

sections.name: researchJobs
sections.title: Research run status and retries
sections.what: Defines the table of research runs for a project, with who started it, status, timing, error, retry count and limit, and a report of verbatim checks. A partial index allows only one queued or running run per project at a time.
sections.why: The one-active-run index stops two research runs from working on the same project at once.
sections.watch_out: That index depends on the status text being exactly queued or running, so a changed spelling in code would break the rule.

sections.name: researchJobSteps
sections.title: Step log inside a research run
sections.what: Defines the table recording each step of a research run, with its attempt number, status, times, input fingerprint, output snapshot, and error.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets failed or retried steps be checked one by one.
sections.watch_out: Steps link to a run by id only, with no foreign key, so orphan step rows can remain if a run is deleted.

sections.name: researchJobDocuments
sections.title: Web pages a research run read
sections.what: Defines the table of documents a research run fetched, with link, domain, authority tier, title, snippet, and the search query that found each one.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps a record of sources used so results can be traced back.
sections.watch_out: The authority tier is an optional number with no range check, so a missing tier is stored as empty rather than a default.

sections.name: realityScanRuns
sections.title: Reality Scan run record
sections.what: Defines the table of Reality Scan runs: what was selected (industries, segments, projects), the mode, status, current stage, timestamps, and any error.
sections.why: The comments explain the selection shape and why the mode is never forced into one value.
sections.watch_out: The scope kind and mode are plain text, so only the code keeps them to valid values.

sections.name: realityScanStageResults
sections.title: Stage results for a Reality Scan run
sections.what: Defines the table storing each stage of a Reality Scan run, with status, start and finish times, a summary, and log text.
sections.why: The comment says a resumed run updates the same stage row, so each stage has one row per run.
sections.watch_out: Only one row per stage per run is allowed, so a retry must update the existing row rather than insert another.

sections.name: lessonsLearntRuns
sections.title: Lessons Learnt run record
sections.what: Defines the table of Lessons Learnt runs, mirroring Reality Scan and adding coverage fields that show how many projects were in scope and processed, and whether the cap cut the list. It also stores the output file path and checksum.
sections.why: The comment says the scope shape is shared so the same selection logic works for both tools.
sections.watch_out: The output file path points to disk, so the file can be missing even when the run shows as finished.

sections.name: lessonsLearntStageResults
sections.title: Stage results for a Lessons Learnt run
sections.what: Defines the table storing each stage of a Lessons Learnt run, with the same fields and one-row-per-stage rule as the Reality Scan version.
sections.why: Likely reason: copied from the Reality Scan design so both tools resume the same way.
sections.watch_out: Its unique rule must stay matched to the run design, or resuming a run can create duplicate stage rows.

sections.name: changeLog
sections.title: History of every field change
sections.what: Defines the change log table, recording each change to a project field with the old and new values, who or what made it, source links, confidence, review state, and the best source tier.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the team see and audit how a project's data changed over time.
sections.watch_out: Review state defaults to approved, so a change saved without a review flag is treated as trusted.

sections.name: schedules
sections.title: Scheduled refresh for each project
sections.what: Defines the table storing how often a project should be checked again, with a recurrence rule, time zone, preferred hour and minute, next and last run times, and an on or off switch.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the app find which projects are due by checking the next run time.
sections.watch_out: Each project has at most one schedule, and the preferred hour has no range check here, so an out-of-range hour can be saved.

sections.name: companies
sections.title: Companies in the database
sections.what: Defines the companies table, with name, type, country, website, description, headquarters, founding date, industry, identifiers from outside sources, and created and updated times.
sections.why: Likely reason: companies are kept apart from projects so one company can appear in many projects.
sections.watch_out: The founding date is stored as text, not as a date, so formats can be inconsistent.

sections.name: companySources
sections.title: Web sources to check for each company
sections.what: Defines the table listing where to look for a company's news or data, with source type, link, an on or off switch, how often to check, last check time, and notes.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the team turn sources on or off without changing code.
sections.watch_out: The crawl frequency is free text, so an unexpected value is stored with no check.

sections.name: companyAliases
sections.title: Alternate names for companies
sections.what: Defines the table of other names a company is known by, recording where each name came from, with a default source of SEED.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets matching find a company even when a source uses a different name.
sections.watch_out: The alias is indexed but not unique by itself, so one alias can point to more than one company.

sections.name: companyProjectLinks
sections.title: Company roles on projects
sections.what: Defines the table linking a company to a project with its role, confidence, first and last seen times, and source link. Each role can appear only once per company and project.
sections.why: Likely reason: records who did what on each project, such as owner or contractor.
sections.watch_out: The role is free text here even though a fixed list of project roles exists, so spelling can drift.

sections.name: discoveryJobs
sections.title: Record of company discovery runs
sections.what: Defines the table of discovery runs, showing the company, status, trigger, timings, error, and a summary of projects scanned, added, updated, linked and skipped as duplicates.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the team see what each discovery run actually did.
sections.watch_out: The summary is stored as a free block, so its fields are checked only by the code that writes it.

sections.name: sources
sections.title: Global list of research sources
sections.what: Defines the table of research sources available to the app, with id, name, type, link, authority tier (defaulting to 3), category, region, industry, an on or off switch, and last fetched time.
sections.why: Likely reason: a shared list lets many projects reuse the same source.
sections.watch_out: The authority tier is a plain number with no range check, so an out-of-range tier would be accepted.

sections.name: projectSources
sections.title: Links between projects and sources
sections.what: Defines a simple table that links projects to sources, using only the two ids.
sections.why: Likely reason: a join table lets one source serve many projects.
sections.watch_out: The table has no uniqueness rule, so the same project and source pair can be stored twice.

sections.name: aiSynthesisCache, insertProjectSchema, insertEvidenceQuoteSchema, insertIssueSchema
sections.title: Saved AI summary cache and input checks
sections.what: Defines the table that caches AI synthesis results by industry and selection, with expiry. It also builds automatic input checks for most of the tables above, with the id removed, so incoming data is checked against column types before saving.
sections.why: The cache key is the same key the in-memory cache uses, so both caches agree on each result.
sections.watch_out: The generated checks drop the id field, so any id a caller sends is ignored.

sections.name: insertAiSynthesisCacheSchema
sections.title: Cache check that keeps the key
sections.what: Builds the input check for the synthesis cache table and keeps the id, because callers supply the cache key themselves.
sections.why: The comment says the key is supplied by the caller, so it cannot be removed.
sections.watch_out: Unlike the other checks, this one accepts an id, so the key format is not checked here.

sections.name: realityScanScopeSchema, RealityScanScope
sections.title: Reality Scan selection check
sections.what: Defines the shape of a Reality Scan selection: lists of industries, industry and segment pairs, and projects, each defaulting to empty. It checks structure only.
sections.why: The comment says at least one of the three must be filled, and the routes perform that check.
sections.watch_out: An empty selection passes this check, so the route check must never be skipped.

sections.name: insertRealityScanRunSchema, insertRealityScanStageResultSchema, Project, InsertProject
sections.title: Checks and types for scan runs and projects
sections.what: Builds the input checks for Reality Scan runs and stage results, and defines the type names for projects and many other tables so code can refer to them.
sections.why: Likely reason: the type names let the editor catch wrong field names.
sections.watch_out: The type names come from the table definitions, so changing a column changes the types wherever they are used.

sections.name: InsertRealityScanStageResult, LessonsLearntScope
sections.title: Scan stage type and shared scope
sections.what: Gives the type for a Reality Scan stage row, and makes the Lessons Learnt scope use the same selection shape.
sections.why: The comment says scope resolution is shared between the two tools.
sections.watch_out: Lessons Learnt inherits every change to the Reality Scan selection shape.

sections.name: insertLessonsLearntRunSchema
sections.title: Check for Lessons Learnt runs
sections.what: Builds the input check for creating a Lessons Learnt run, leaving out the generated id and the timestamps.
sections.why: Likely reason: the database fills in the id and timestamps automatically.
sections.watch_out: Coverage and output fields are also checked, so a run created without them must allow them to be empty.

sections.name: insertLessonsLearntStageResultSchema, LessonsLearntRun, InsertLessonsLearntRun, LessonsLearntStageResult
sections.title: Lessons Learnt stage and run types
sections.what: Builds the input check for Lessons Learnt stage rows and defines the type names for Lessons Learnt runs and stage rows.
sections.why: Likely reason: follows the same pattern as the other tools, so the code stays consistent.
sections.watch_out: Changing a column in the table definition changes these types, so callers may need updating.

sections.name: partiesSchema
sections.title: Check for parties list
sections.what: Checks that the parties field is a list where each entry has a role and a name, both containing at least one character.
sections.why: Likely reason: stops blank party entries from being saved.
sections.watch_out: Only the shape is checked, so a party with an unknown role word is still accepted.

sections.name: supplyChainSchema
sections.title: Check for supply chain list
sections.what: Checks that supply chain data is a list of entries, each with a component, supplier and status as text.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps supply chain rows in one consistent shape.
sections.watch_out: Empty text is allowed here, unlike the parties check, so blank suppliers can be saved.

sections.name: variancesSchema
sections.title: Check for cost and schedule overrun
sections.what: Checks the overrun record: planned and actual cost, percentage change, cost reason, planned and actual duration, months of delay, and schedule reason. The whole record may be empty.
sections.why: Likely reason: many projects have no overrun data, so the record is allowed to be empty.
sections.watch_out: Numbers are checked only as numbers, so zero or negative delays are accepted.

sections.name: similarProjectsSchema
sections.title: Check for similar project list
sections.what: Checks that similar projects are a list, with each entry holding an id, a name, and a reason for the match.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives each similar project a stated reason that users can read.
sections.watch_out: The reason text can be empty, so a match can be saved with no explanation.

sections.name: citationLocatorSchema
sections.title: Check for source position
sections.what: Checks a citation's position marker: a type that must be a text fragment, a PDF page, or an anchor, with an optional value.
sections.why: Likely reason: tells the viewer where in the source to scroll.
sections.watch_out: Only the three listed types are accepted, so a new position type needs this list updated first.

sections.name: citationItemSchema, citationsSchema, CitationItem
sections.title: Check for source citations
sections.what: Checks one citation, with id, title, link and optional details, then checks a list of citations, and defines the matching type.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps every citation in the same shape across the app.
sections.watch_out: Only id, title and link are required, so a citation with no publisher or date is accepted.

sections.name: COMPANY_TYPES
sections.title: Allowed company types
sections.what: Lists the twelve allowed company types, such as owner, EPC contractor, supplier, regulator, and media.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed list keeps company types consistent across the database and screens.
sections.watch_out: The companies table stores type as free text, so the database does not enforce this list.

sections.name: PROJECT_ROLES
sections.title: Allowed project roles
sections.what: Lists the seventeen roles a company can play on a project, such as operator, EPC contractor, reactor vendor, and regulator.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed role list keeps role names consistent.
sections.watch_out: The company link table stores role as free text, so this list is not enforced there.

sections.name: ROLE_LABELS
sections.title: Display names for roles and types
sections.what: Maps each role and company type code to a short display label and a one-line definition, so screens can show readable names.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps display wording separate from the codes stored in the database.
sections.watch_out: This map includes some company types that are not in the company type list, so the two can drift apart.

summary: Defines every database table the app uses, with column types and indexes, and builds the input checks and type names the code uses for them.
purpose: Keeps the database layout for projects, research, scanning, companies and sources in one place, from which the input checks are generated.
why: Likely reason: writing each table once in code keeps the database definition and the input checks in step.
how: First the file imports the database and checking libraries. Next it defines the main projects table and its indexes. Then it defines the supporting tables for quotes, issues, scorecards, gates, stories, glossary, milestones, updates, technology, SKUs and research. After that come the Reality Scan, Lessons Learnt, change log, schedule, company and source tables. Last, it generates input checks for most tables with the id removed, and defines the shared shapes for lists and citations, plus the allowed company types and project roles and their labels.
inputs: Data written by ingest, research, scanning, and user actions. The table definitions take no input when the app runs.
outputs: Table definitions used to build the database, input checks used by the code, and type names used by the editor.
risks: A column change here must be matched by a database migration, and the comments refer to numbered migrations such as 0010. If they disagree, the app and the database will fail or behave differently. Several free-text columns should be fixed lists, so bad values can be saved.
debug: If saving fails with a type error or a missing field, compare the field with its column here and with the latest migration. If an input check rejects valid data, check whether the field is required here. If a budget looks wrong on screen, check the column type, since the older budget column is a float and the planned and actual budget columns are exact numbers.
